deepseek_avx2_finding.question: Should a DeepSeek-V4.1-specific AVX2 CPU kernel be written now?
deepseek_avx2_finding.answer: Not yet. It is a measurable answer, not a preference: the only DeepSeek CPU code that exists is candidate selection, and on this CPU it is dominated by std::sort, not by vectorizable scoring.
deepseek_avx2_finding.geometry: 40,000 rows, block size 8, 2048 blocks wanted, k 512, the model's real decode geometry, pinned to one core with taskset
deepseek_avx2_finding.speedup_from_avx2_flags: about 9 percent, identical checksums, so the AVX2 and generic builds already agree bit for bit on this input
deepseek_avx2_finding.interpretation: Stage two is about 80 percent of the cost and it sorts 16384 candidate rows to keep 512. The block-maximum scan, the only genuinely vectorizable loop in the pair, costs about 1.7 percent of a stage-one call. An AVX2 rewrite of the scan would optimize the part that is not the bottleneck; the leverage is an algorithmic change such as a bounded top-k heap or a partial sort, which is format-independent and is therefore not AVX2-specific.
deepseek_avx2_finding.next_boundary: The next CPU boundary is the RESMP-owned pack format and its inverse, plus the safetensors layout planner. Until a pack layout is fixed there is no weight row layout for an AVX2 expert kernel to target, and writing one now would be speculative work against a layout that is about to be decided.

non_claims: No Qwen3.8-Flash-Next model was downloaded, converted, quantized, loaded, or run; the engine binary was exercised only through its self-tests and its help text.
No DeepSeek-V4.1 pack, quantizer, expert kernel, or runtime path was implemented or benchmarked; the timings above measure the existing reference only.
No CUDA kernel was executed on either RTX 3090 Ti; no GPU inference, no VRAM model placement, and no throughput number is claimed.
The candidate-selection timings are single-core, same-process, and are not a model throughput claim; they compare two builds of one function on one host.
